questions.question: In Dante's 'Inferno', who serves as the narrator's guide through Hell?
questions.explanation: The ancient Roman poet Virgil acts as Dante's guide through the nine circles of Hell.
questions.funFact: The 'Inferno' is just the first part of a larger epic poem called 'The Divine Comedy', which also includes 'Purgatorio' and 'Paradiso'.

questions.question: What narrative technique is prominently used by James Joyce in 'Ulysses' and Virginia Woolf in 'Mrs. Dalloway'?
questions.explanation: Stream of consciousness attempts to capture the unfiltered, continuous flow of a character's thoughts and feelings.
questions.funFact: James Joyce's 'Ulysses' takes place entirely on a single day: June 16, 1904, a date now celebrated globally by fans as 'Bloomsday'.

questions.question: In Toni Morrison's 'Beloved', who or what is Beloved?
options: A ghost/reincarnation of Sethe's murdered child
An escaped slave who helps the family
questions.explanation: Beloved is the physical manifestation of the traumatic past, representing the infant Sethe killed to save her from slavery.
questions.funFact: Morrison based the novel on the true story of Margaret Garner, an enslaved African American woman who escaped to Ohio in 1856.

questions.question: What is the literary term for a genre where magical elements are a natural part of an otherwise mundane, realistic environment?
questions.explanation: Magical realism blends fantastical elements seamlessly into real-world settings, famously used by Latin American authors.
questions.funFact: Gabriel García Márquez said his tone for 'One Hundred Years of Solitude' was inspired by the deadpan way his grandmother used to tell fantastic stories.

questions.question: In Herman Melville's 'Moby-Dick', what is the name of Captain Ahab's ship?
questions.explanation: The Pequod is the doomed whaling ship commanded by the obsessed Captain Ahab.
questions.funFact: When 'Moby-Dick' was first published in London, the epilogue was accidentally omitted, leaving readers confused as to how the narrator survived to tell the tale.

questions.question: Who undergoes a bizarre transformation into a giant insect in Franz Kafka's 'The Metamorphosis'?
questions.explanation: Gregor Samsa wakes up one morning to find himself transformed into a 'monstrous vermin'.
questions.funFact: Kafka strictly forbade his publisher from ever illustrating the insect on the book's cover, wanting it to remain ambiguous.

questions.question: Which novel features the complicated Compson family and is famously divided into four sections with different narrators?
questions.explanation: William Faulkner's modernist masterpiece uses multiple narrators, including the intellectually disabled Benjy, to tell the story of a falling Southern aristocratic family.
questions.funFact: The title is taken from a famous soliloquy in Shakespeare's 'Macbeth': 'It is a tale told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, signifying nothing.'

questions.question: In Fyodor Dostoevsky's 'Crime and Punishment', what justifies Raskolnikov's decision to commit murder in his own mind?
options: He is starving and needs money
He believes he is an 'extraordinary' man above moral law
He is ordered to by a secret society
questions.explanation: Raskolnikov develops a theory that certain extraordinary individuals have the right to commit crimes if it serves a higher purpose.
questions.funFact: Dostoevsky wrote the novel in a frantic rush to pay off massive gambling debts.

questions.question: Who wrote 'The Canterbury Tales'?
questions.explanation: Chaucer wrote this collection of stories told by pilgrims traveling to the shrine of Saint Thomas Becket.
questions.funFact: Chaucer originally planned for each of the 30 pilgrims to tell four stories each (120 total), but he died having completed only 24.

questions.question: In Joseph Conrad's 'Heart of Darkness', what are Kurtz's famous last words?
options: 'A horse! A horse! My kingdom for a horse!'
'It is a far, far better thing that I do...'
questions.explanation: Kurtz whispers 'The horror! The horror!' before dying, reflecting on the darkness of human nature he experienced in the Congo.
questions.funFact: The novella heavily inspired the 1979 film 'Apocalypse Now', which adapted the story from colonial Africa to the Vietnam War.

questions.question: What is the term for a narrator whose credibility has been seriously compromised, either intentionally or unintentionally?
questions.explanation: An unreliable narrator may be deceptive, misinformed, mentally unstable, or naive, forcing the reader to question the truth of the story.
questions.funFact: Agatha Christie famously used a deceitful unreliable narrator in 'The Murder of Roger Ackroyd', shocking contemporary readers.

questions.question: Miguel de Cervantes' 'Don Quixote' is often considered the first modern novel. What does Quixote mistake for giants?
questions.explanation: Don Quixote attacks windmills, believing them to be ferocious giants, giving rise to the idiom 'tilting at windmills'.
questions.funFact: Cervantes came up with the idea for the novel while serving a sentence in a Spanish debtor's prison.

questions.question: Which poet is known for heavily employing 'enjambment' and unconventional capitalization, as seen in poems like 'anyone lived in a pretty how town'?
questions.explanation: E.E. Cummings was famous for his radical experimentation with form, punctuation, syntax, and spelling.
questions.funFact: Cummings actually spent several months in a French military prison during WWI due to a bureaucratic mix-up, an experience he turned into his novel 'The Enormous Room'.

questions.question: What famous opening line begins Jane Austen's 'Pride and Prejudice'?
options: 'Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.'
'It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.'
questions.explanation: This satirical opening perfectly sets up the novel's themes of marriage, wealth, and societal expectations.
questions.funFact: Jane Austen initially titled the manuscript 'First Impressions' before revising it years later.

questions.question: In 'The Awakening' by Kate Chopin, Edna Pontellier's suicide at the end is often interpreted by critics as an act of:
questions.explanation: Feminist critics often argue Edna's drowning is her final refusal to compromise her independence to fit the suffocating roles of wife and mother.
questions.funFact: The book was so controversial for its frank depiction of female sexual desire that it was banned from libraries in Chopin's hometown of St. Louis.

questions.question: What literary movement, prominent after WWI, features fragmentation, loss of absolute truth, and a break from traditional forms (e.g., T.S. Eliot's 'The Waste Land')?
questions.explanation: Modernism arose as a response to the devastating industrialization and world wars, rejecting the certainty of Enlightenment thinking.
questions.funFact: T.S. Eliot's 'The Waste Land' was heavily edited by his friend and fellow poet Ezra Pound, who cut the poem's length nearly in half.

questions.question: Which novel by Ralph Ellison utilizes jazz and blues motifs to structure its narrative about the African American experience?
options: Go Tell It on the Mountain
questions.explanation: 'Invisible Man' is heavily influenced by musical improvisation and the rhythm of jazz, reflecting the protagonist's chaotic journey.
questions.funFact: Ellison was an accomplished trumpet player who studied classical music at the Tuskegee Institute before becoming a writer.

questions.question: What does the 'A' worn by Hester Prynne stand for in Nathaniel Hawthorne's 'The Scarlet Letter'?
questions.explanation: Hester is forced to wear the letter 'A' as punishment for her affair and illegitimate child in Puritan Boston.
questions.funFact: Nathaniel Hawthorne added the 'W' to his last name (originally Hathorne) to distance himself from his great-great-grandfather, who was a harsh judge during the Salem witch trials.

questions.question: In Leo Tolstoy's 'Anna Karenina', what mode of transportation is heavily symbolic and fatally linked to the protagonist?
questions.explanation: Trains symbolize the destructive force of modernization in the novel, and Anna ultimately throws herself under one.
questions.funFact: Tolstoy initially intended for Anna to be a highly unsympathetic character, but as he wrote, he grew to pity and understand her.

questions.question: In Samuel Beckett's play 'Waiting for Godot', who is Godot?
options: He never appears and his identity is never explained
questions.explanation: Godot never arrives. The play is a cornerstone of the 'Theatre of the Absurd', emphasizing the meaninglessness of human existence.
questions.funFact: When asked who or what Godot actually was, Beckett famously replied, 'If I knew, I would have said so in the play.'
